common_name: SunRich Lemon Sunflower (Pollen-Free Single-Stem Pale Yellow Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; succession sow every 1-2 weeks through summer since the crop matures all at once.

directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep on 6-9 inch spacing in full sun. SunRich Lemon grows as a single unbranched stem bred for uniform height and bloom timing, producing pale, soft lemon-yellow petals around a dark center disk that offer a gentler, more pastel look than the deep golds typical of most cut-flower sunflowers. Because the flowers are pollen-free, they're a clean choice for mixed arrangements and won't stain fabric or drop pollen on tablecloths. Plan on harvesting the entire planting within a narrow window, roughly 55-65 days after sowing, and cut when petals have just started to open for maximum vase life.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Kniola's Black Knight Morning Glory (Deep Purple Ruffled Morning Glory)

planting.note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost; morning glories resent transplanting.

directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Kniola's Black Knight bears small, ruffled, semi-double flowers in the deepest purple of any commonly grown morning glory, reading nearly black in low light and offering a moodier, more dramatic alternative to the classic sky-blue morning glory palette. Like other Ipomoea purpurea types it opens fresh each dawn and closes by early afternoon, climbing vigorously by twining stems that can quickly cover a trellis or fence in a single season. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set to prevent unwanted volunteers the following year, since morning glories self-sow readily in warm climates.

Flying Saucers produces large flowers marbled and striped in blue and white in an unpredictable, painterly pattern that varies from bloom to bloom, so no two flowers look quite the same, an appealing novelty on an otherwise typical fast-growing, twining vine. Like other Ipomoea tricolor types it opens fresh each dawn and closes by early afternoon, blooming most heavily as days shorten in late summer and fall. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set to prevent unwanted volunteers the following year, since morning glories self-sow readily in warm climates.
